story: The donkey belonged to a merchant who did not pay enough attention and worked on it. So the donkey Zeus searched for a new lord. After Zeus had warned the donkey that he would regret this request, he had it sold to a bricklayer. The donkey soon discovered that the stones he had to carry were much heavier than those of the merchant and asked Zeus again for a new master. The god left the donkey one last time and sold it to a tanner, who treated it worse than its previous owners. So the donkey whispered: 'I would have been better if I had died of hunger or fatigue at one of my former masters, because the new one will skin me after my death to serve me for him'.

story: A sniper had built his nest in the spring on a freshly saturated wheat field. Their children grew up when the farmer, looking at his harvest, said: 'I will ask all my friends and neighbours to help me with the harvest'. One of the young sheep asked his mother if they should move to a new place for safety reasons. "Not yet," she replied; "a man who only asks his friends to help him harvest is not quite ready for it." A few days later, the farmer noticed that the wheat was bulky and said: 'Well, I will hire as many workers as possible and harvest the wheat myself'. When she heard those words, the sniper said to her children: 'It is time for us to move - a man who no longer trusts his friends but who will reap the field himself will continue his plans'.

One of the young snipes asked his mother whether they should move to a new place for safety. story: One day a thief had to rent a room in an inn and stayed for some time hoping to steal something to pay the bill. He finally came to the conclusion that the innkeeper was wearing a new, fancy coat, which would undoubtedly have a good price. The thief sat down with the innkeeper and talked to him. After some time, he ran over and howled like a wolf. Surprised, the innkeeper asked why he should do so. The thief replied: "I say unto you, but ye shall keep my garments, or I will tear them apart. I do not know when I began to bend this way or what caused this change of behavior, but I do know that if I am to bend three times in a row, I will turn into a wolf and attack anyone who is in sight. When he said this, he screamed a second time and laughed. The innkeeper looked on in alarm and wanted to escape the thief. When he noticed this, the thief put a hand on the innkeeper's coat and asked him to stay for a while and hold his clothes so that they would not be torn if he turned into a wolf. As he said, the thief smiled a third time and screamed particularly horribly. This frightened the innkeeper and escaped the thief as quickly as possible. The thief, satisfied with this result, took the mantle and left the inn and never came again.

Eventually, he noticed that the innkeeper was wearing a new, fancy coat that would undoubtedly fetch a good price. So the thief sat down with the innkeeper and engaged him in conversation. After some time, he yawned in an exaggerated fashion and howled like a wolf. Surprised, the innkeeper inquired why he would do such a thing. The thief replied: "I will tell you, but you’ll have to hold my clothes or I will tear them to pieces. I’m not sure when I started yawning like this or what caused this change in behavior, I only know that when I yawn three times in a row, I will turn into a wolf and attack anyone in sight." Once he said this, he immediately yawned and howled a second time. The innkeeper looked visibly alarmed and, planning to run away from the thief, started to stand up. Noticing this, the thief put a hand on the innkeeper’s coat and asked him to stay a while longer to hold his clothes, so that they won’t get torn when he transforms into a wolf. Just as he was saying this, the thief yawned a third time and howled in a particularly terrifying manner. This scared the innkeeper greatly and, shrugging off his coat to escape the thief's grip, he ran away as fast as he could. The thief, happy with this outcome, took the coat and left the inn never to return.

Thus, Zeus placed a log into the toads’ pond, assuming that it would suffice for such simple creatures. Initially terrified of the log, the toads soon realized that it remained motionless and posed no danger. Seeing the log as unfit to be their ruler, the toads petitioned Zeus once more. Thus, he sent an eel to govern them. As the eel was good-natured and made no demands of the toads, they felt misunderstood by the deity and once again asked him to provide them with a proper ruler. Annoyed, Zeus sent a heron to live in their pond, who soon ate all of the toads.

Eventually he invented a clever trick of playing the bulls against each other, and as soon as they separated, the tiger attacked them and devoured them one by one.

story: After visiting places around the world, the traveller often boasted about the various services he provided when he returned to his home town. He once claimed that he jumped so high during a visit to Tokyo that no other person could ever jump half as high. To lend more credibility to his words, he went on to say that many people could be summoned in Tokyo to testify to their deeds. One of the spectators pointed out that this is not necessary if the traveller simply jumps in front of himself, as he did in Tokyo.

story: In the garden a rose grew next to an amaranth. One day the Amaranth said to her neighbour: "Your beauty and your sweet scent are to be envied! I am not surprised that you are loved by everyone.' The Rose replied with sadness in her voice: "My friend, my flower only lasts for a short time. At some point my petals will fade and I will perish. It is eternal, for your flowers do not fade away, even when they are cut.'

You, on the other hand, are everlasting, as your flowers do not fade even when cut."

story: A deer fled to a barn and hid in a haystack, only visible from the outside with the horns. The stable was soon visited by hunters chasing their dogs. The stable boys moaning after dinner asked them if they had seen a deer, but when they looked around, none of them could see the deer. After some time, the stablemaster came and asked what was strange outside. When the stable boys examined the pile, they quickly discovered the deer and killed it.
gold_story: In an attempt to escape a pack of pursuing dogs, a stag fled inside a stable and hid himself in a pile of hay, with only the tips of his horns visible to the outside. Soon, the stable was visited by hunters trailing their dogs. They asked the stable boys, who were resting after their dinner, if they had seen a stag, but looking around the stable, neither were able to spot the stag. After some time, the master of the stable came in and, pointing at the pile of hay, asked what the two strange things sticking out of it were. When the stable boys examined the pile, they quickly discovered the stag and killed him.

story: When he crossed a stream, the raccoon was swept away by the strong current and pushed into a deep ravine, where he could not move because of his injuries. Soon a swarm of blood-sucking flies found him and attacked his skin. Some time later, the raccoon was discovered by a sparrowhawk, who asked her to scare away the flies that torture him. The raccoon replied weakly: "Please don't bother them. The flies you see drank a lot of my blood and no longer bite me much. If you fear them, new flies come, hungry and suck me dry.'

"What a sad life you live, a strange creature," said the locust of locusts, "while I can jump around in my spare time, you're caught in your shell and can't move beyond your brilliant tail." The Chryssalis heard the unpleasant comments, but did not answer. A few days later, the grasshopper returned to Crysalis, but found only an empty shell. He wondered what had happened and suddenly felt overshadowed by the shadowy wings of a magnificent butterfly. "I am it, your beloved friend! So the butterfly said to the grasshopper: 'Please congratulate you again on your superiority, but only as long as you can reach me'. Nevertheless, the butterfly rose to the sky and was soon invisible to the grasshopper.

story: Little bush, why do you not stand as high as I do?  asked the oak of the nearby bush. Bush replied, "I am happy with what I am. Moreover, I am sure that you are more powerful than I ever hoped, but I think I am safer." The oak laughed at the shrub's word: "Safe? Who could threaten me or throw me to the floor?" Shortly afterwards, the forest was hit by a storm and the oak was destroyed without great effort. The bush, on the other hand, bowed to the storm and stood upright as it passed.

story: On his way home from a successful hunt, the hunter came across a fisherman carrying a bucket full of fish. Since the hunter loved some of the fish and the fisherman wanted some of the meat of the hunter, they agreed on a fair exchange. Both were pleased and repeated the same exchange day after day. A neighbour who had discovered that he could trade his goods said: 'If you keep doing that every day, you will soon lose all pleasure in exchanging because it becomes the norm and you want to keep your reward'.

Next day, the goats were unable to go to the pasture due to a heavy storm, so the goatherd supplied them with hay for the day, giving the wild goats plenty of food to entice them to stay, while only giving just enough to the rest of the flock. The day after, just as the goatherd opened the enclosure to bring the goats to the pasture, the wild goats stormed out and ran away as fast as they could. Upset, the goatherd shouted after them, accusing them of ingratitude. The goats replied: "The very reason why we do not want to stay is that you gave us more food than your own flock! If we stayed and some new goats came along, you would treat us badly just to impress the new arrivals."

story: One winter, a farmer found a frozen snake in the snow. He took it up and put it in his chest. The snake was quickly revived by the heat and bites its rescuer according to its natural instincts, which fatally injured the peasant dog. In his last breath the farmer screamed: "That is what I must apologize to a rogue!"
gold_story: One winter a farmhand found a frozen serpent lying in the snow. Taking pity on her, he picked her up and placed her in his bosom. The serpent was quickly revived by the warmth, and bit his saviour following her natural instincts, wounding the farmhand mortally. With his last breath, the farmhand cried: "This is what I get for pitying a scoundrel!"

He flew on the bottle at great speed, crashed against the board and was seriously injured. Both wings broke by the impact, and he fell to the ground, but caught by a passer-by.

story: The coyote discovered a lamb that was far from their hearth, and decided to justify the lamb’s right to eat it, rather than simply attacking it. So he said to the lamb: "I remember you insulted me in a very serious way last year!" The Lamb replied that she was not even born at that time. So the coyote had another lie: 'Believe, you are grazing on my pasture!' The lamb, however, replied that it never ate grass because it was young. Exasperated the coyote said, "Well, then you drink from my well!" The lamb replied that it was drinking only breast milk. The coyote took the lamb and swallowed it with the words: 'Well, despite your convincing arguments, I decide not to stay without dinner'.
gold_story: The coyote, having noticed a lamb that strayed far away from her flock, decided that he should justify to the lamb his right to eat her, instead of simply attacking her. Therefore, he said to the lamb: "I remember that you insulted me most gravely last year!". The lamb replied that she was not even born back then. The coyote thus came up with another lie: "Clearly, you are grazing on my pasture!" The lamb, however, retorted that she has never even tasted grass, due to her young age. Exasperated, the coyote said: "Well, then you’re drinking from my well!" In response, the lamb pointed out that she only drank her mother’s milk. Fed up, the coyote picked up the lamb and swallowed her, saying: "Well, despite your convincing arguments, I choose not to remain without dinner."

story: The horse and the elk argued, and so the horse went to the forester and asked for help to attack the elk again. The woodman agreed and said: "If you want my help, I must place this iron between your pines to guide you with the reins. I must also help you so that I am firmly on the road to the enemy." The horse agreed and was quickly pressed and tamed. After the elk was defeated, the horse asked the forester to take away his riding clothes.
gold_story: The horse and the moose had a fight, so the horse went to the woodsman and asked him for help in getting back at the moose. The woodsman agreed, saying: "If you want my help, I will have to place this iron between your jaws to be able to guide you with these reins. I must also saddle you, so that I can keep steady as we pursue your enemy." The horse agreed and was quickly saddled and bridled. After the moose was vanquished, the horse demanded that the woodsman remove the riding equipment, to which the woodsman replied that he prefers to keep the horse just as he is.

story: Tired of becoming so timid and anxious, the rabbits decided to end their life together by jumping from a high cliff into a deep sea below. As their large group approached the edge of the cliff, the toads on the shores of the lake were alarmed by the sound of their feet and fled quickly to safety. When one of the rabbits observed the flight of the toads, one rabbit ordered the other to stop: "Wait, my friends! Perhaps we should not allow our plan to override everyone, because there are obviously creatures that are even more afraid than we are.'
gold_story: The rabbits, tired of being so timid and scared all of the time, decided to collectively end their lives by jumping off a tall cliff into a deep lake below. As their large group approached the edge of the cliff, the toads living on the banks of the lake became alarmed by the sound of their feet and quickly fled to safety. Observing the flight of the toads, one of the rabbits ordered the others to stop: "Wait, my friends! Maybe we should not go through with our plan, afer all, as there are clearly creatures who are even more easily scared than we are."

story: The silk robe received an order from Tigress for twenty metres of finest silk and began to work on the loom as soon as possible. Some time later a spider came by and wanted to rent a loom nearby. The spider started working on her own project and was soon finished. The spider observed the methodical work of the silkworm and noticed when leaving: "Look at how large and tender my net is! And I took a fraction of the time to turn it that it would have cost you. You must admit that I am a much better worker than you could ever be." The silkworm replied: "Be quiet, you distract me. After all, your websites are nothing more than simple traps that are destroyed and washed away as useless rubbish as soon as they are seen. By contrast, the fruits of my work are appreciated by kings around the world.'
gold_story: The silkworm received an order for twenty yards of her finest silk from the tigress and, aiming to finish the order as soon as possible, started working at her loom. Some time later, a spider stopped by and wanted to rent a web-room nearby, to which the silkworm agreed. The spider started working on her own project and was soon finished. Observing the methodical labor of the silkworm, the spider remarked, as she was leaving: "Look at how great and delicate my webs are! The silkworm replied: "Be quiet - you’re distracting me. In the end, your webs are nothing more than basic traps, destroyed and brushed away as useless dirt whenever they are seen. Soon a hunter came with his dogs and asked the forester if he was looking past a raccoon. The forester replied that he had not done so, but he pointed repeatedly at the hut as he spoke. The hunter, however, forgot his signs and continued hunting at the hut. When the air was clear, the raccoon left the hut and made his way, when the forester said to him: "How unworthy of you without a word of thanks, although I saved your life". The raccoon replied: 'I would have thanked you if your actions had been as good as your words and your speech had not been betrayed by your hands'.

story: Zeus declared that he would make the most beautiful of the birds king over the others and gave him a day for it. In preparation, all birds retreated to a lake shore to wash and care for their feathers. Among them was a bird that knew that its weak plumage would not make it king. So he waited until the other birds had left the shore, gathered the most beautiful feathers they had left behind and moulded them into a dress that made him appear more beautiful than the rest of the birds. On the scheduled day, all the birds presented themselves to Zeus, who recognized the cock as the most beautiful among them. But as he was about to crown the new bird king, the other birds cut off his beak and revealed his true boring plumage.
